title: P-Trap Leaking Under Sink: How to Fix It
metaDescription: Water pooling in the cabinet under your sink? Here's how to find and fix a leaking P-trap — usually a loose slip nut, not a cracked pipe.
symptom: Water drips or pools under the sink, usually noticed when you open the cabinet doors, especially after running the faucet or draining a full sink.
partsNeeded: Replacement P-trap assembly (if the pipe itself is cracked)

steps.heading: Clear out the cabinet and place a bucket
steps.body: Remove everything from under the sink and put a bucket or shallow pan directly under the P-trap (the U-shaped pipe) to catch water and debris during the fix.

steps.heading: Find exactly where it's leaking
steps.body: Dry everything off with a towel, then run water and watch closely. Leaks almost always show up at one of the slip-nut connections (the ribbed plastic/metal collars where pipe sections join) rather than from a crack in the pipe itself.

steps.heading: Tighten the slip nuts by hand first
steps.body: Try hand-tightening the slip nut at the leaking joint a quarter turn. Loose connections are the most common cause and often need nothing more than this.

steps.heading: Disassemble and inspect the washer if it still leaks
steps.body: If hand-tightening doesn't stop it, use channel-lock pliers to loosen the slip nut, slide it back, and check the washer inside. A cracked, flattened, or missing washer is the next most common culprit.

steps.heading: Replace the washer and reassemble
steps.body: Install a new washer (bring the old one to the store to match size/shape), make sure the pipe ends are pushed together fully and square, then hand-tighten the slip nut followed by a quarter turn with pliers — snug, not forceful.

steps.heading: Run water and check for drips
steps.body: Run the faucet for a couple minutes and check every joint, then let a full sink drain at once (the higher flow rate reveals leaks a slow trickle won't).

whenToCallAPro: If the pipe itself (not a joint) is cracked, if the leak is coming from where the trap connects to the wall drain, or if tightening/rewashering the joints doesn't stop it, call a plumber — a damaged wall drain fitting isn't a DIY-friendly repair.
safetyWarnings: Don't overtighten slip nuts with pliers — plastic P-trap fittings crack under too much torque, turning a small leak into a bigger repair.
Standing water under a sink near outlets or extension cords is a shock hazard — dry the area and check for nearby electrical before working.
